doc.title: Lisa Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 22, 2021

title: The three-stringed bass and busking group
summary: Story of the school-closet double bass that Harry fitted with three strings for Nicki.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: The three stringed bass, so Harry, the bass player who gave me that Sidney Bechet tape, he played bass and because I was like okay, this is it — we already had a little busking group together and, “Nicki, we need, you can’t play flute in my group. You have to play tuba or bass if you want to be in my jazz group.” I was forming a jazz group. And there was a double bass that had no bridge or any strings or anything, in the school closet at the high school, in the closet at the high school. We brought it home, Harry put three strings on it and a bridge, and I think according to Nicki like he shaved too much off the bridge and the strings were hitting the fingerboard. But he said, his theory was you can’t hear the E string anyway so there was no point having an E string. So he always played the three stringed bass. So for the first couple of months Nicki was playing an E stringed bass, I mean a three stringed bass, until we went to a music camp where someone put an E string on the bass for her.
Yeah. “You can’t hear the E string anyway.”

Yeah. There are so many things that happen to young musicians along the way up and I think busking and, you know I was reading your bios and things on your website and it sounds like you were in and out of a number of bands, and there’s a lot of education that goes on in that.
